prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Smart-city demonstration roads Road lighting for smart-city demonstration roads has no special requirements and may refer to other road types. 126 4.1.7 Public Transport 1. Location of bus stops A. Bus stops shall generally be set in conjunction with rail transit stations, shopping malls, hospitals, schools, residential areas, and other buildings, close to pedestrian entrances and exits, so as to reduce the walking distance for passengers boarding buses. 2. Setting of bus bays A. Bus bays should be set on arterial roads; on secondary arterial roads, whether to set bus bays shall be determined according to bus traffic volume. B. When bus traffic volume is low, straight curbside stops may be adopted after demonstration. Where land is constrained, bus platforms in reconstruction, expansion, or major repair projects may be set in conjunction with existing conditions. 3. Other requirements for bus stop setting A. The location of bus bays shall not encroach on pedestrian and non-motorized traffic space, and shall not affect the safety and order of pedestrian and non-motorized traffic. B. To avoid conflicts between buses stopping and non-motorized vehicles, the road may be locally widened, with the non-motorized lane set on the outside of the bus platform (bus shelter, stop sign, etc.). Where conditions are limited, the bus platform may be set within the facility belt of the roadside belt, and measures to slow non-motorized vehicles shall be taken. Figure 4.1-17 Design drawing combining bus stops and non-motorized lanes C. For roads in old urban areas where space is severely constrained, when curbside bus stops have to occupy the non-motorized lane, a motor-vehicle/non-motor-vehicle separation barrier shall be set upstream and downstream of the stop, and a slowing/yielding zone shall be set on the non-motorized lane. 4. Bus shelter setting A. Bus shelters should adopt an integral stainless-steel frame structure and be equipped with bus stop seats, light boxes, display screens, intelligent monitoring, lighting, illumination enhancement, and other facilities. Lighting and illumination enhancement shall meet relevant requirements. 127 Figure 4.1-18 Example of bus shelter and bus seat 5. Metro feeder connections A. In conjunction with bus planning, reduce long-distance co-linear routes with the metro, and increase vertical bus feeder routes and “Z”-shaped bus feeder routes; in conjunction with metro traffic recovery design, adjust the locations of bus stops to meet the needs of feeder bus routes and transfer distance requirements. B. According to station functions and passenger flow conditions, appropriately arrange non-motorized vehicle parking spaces at each station, and implement unified and orderly parking management in areas with concentrated demand for non-motorized vehicle parking.

As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Purpose of Formulation Under the macro guidance of the “General Provisions,” these Detailed Rules aim at the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads, and are expanded and implemented from four directions: human-oriented, quality-oriented, distinctive, and intelligent. They interpret the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads in the form of colorful labels, and create urban colorful roads unique to Suzhou. ➢ Human-oriented: Starting from the users of Suzhou’s urban roads, and taking the public’s experience of urban road space as the benchmark, fully consider the comfort, safety, and convenience of public activities, and realize the value shift from “vehicle-centered” to “people-centered.” ➢ Quality-oriented: Vigorously improve the travel quality of people and vehicle traffic in Suzhou, and emphasize the public space function of roads. Appropriately raise the standards for urban road design, construction, and maintenance, extend road service life, and improve users’ comfort of experience. Reflect a road construction level of high appearance and high standards, with attention to detail and control. ➢ Distinctive: Adapt measures to local conditions, and through the embedding of Suzhou-style elements and the creation of road characteristic scenes, highlight Suzhou’s distinctive urban character of integration between tradition and modernity, so that urban roads become an important carrier and display space for the “Jiangnan culture” brand, and continue the city’s historical and cultural lineage. ➢ Intelligent: Deploy intelligent sensing devices along the roadside, together with cloud service platforms, computing and communication facilities, and through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, realize a travel experience of deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, assist safe driving and autonomous driving, and create demonstration roads with Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. 2. Smart-city demonstration roads Road lighting for smart-city demonstration roads has no special requirements and may refer to other road types. 126 4.1.7 Public Transport 1. Location of bus stops A. Bus stops shall generally be set in conjunction with rail transit stations, shopping malls, hospitals, schools, residential areas, and other buildings, close to pedestrian entrances and exits, so as to reduce the walking distance for passengers boarding buses. 2. Setting of bus bays A. Bus bays should be set on arterial roads; on secondary arterial roads, whether to set bus bays shall be determined according to bus traffic volume. B. When bus traffic volume is low, straight curbside stops may be adopted after demonstration. Where land is constrained, bus platforms in reconstruction, expansion, or major repair projects may be set in conjunction with existing conditions. 3. Other requirements for bus stop setting A. The location of bus bays shall not encroach on pedestrian and non-motorized traffic space, and shall not affect the safety and order of pedestrian and non-motorized traffic. B. To avoid conflicts between buses stopping and non-motorized vehicles, the road may be locally widened, with the non-motorized lane set on the outside of the bus platform (bus shelter, stop sign, etc.). Where conditions are limited, the bus platform may be set within the facility belt of the roadside belt, and measures to slow non-motorized vehicles shall be taken. (4) Transportation scenarios. Pedestrian crossing scenario. Give priority to ensuring safe and convenient pedestrian crossing. For large urban intersections and traffic roads of larger scale, adopt smaller curb radii and prudently set up... Set channelized facilities to shorten crossing distances at intersections; bicycle waiting areas may be provided in areas where conditions permit. For residential streets with heavy pedestrian flows, compact intersections or raised intersections may be adopted to reduce vehicle speeds. Public transit travel scenarios. Around urban bus stops, priority should be given to traffic transfer and the needs of special groups. Enrich the service functions of the stop area, strengthen integrated bus stop design, and coordinate the layout of shelters, trash bins, public toilets, and other facilities, while providing barrier-free ramps. Improve the convenience of bus transfers and use: bus stops should be located as close as possible to community entrances and metro entrances, with parking areas for non-motorized vehicles and shared bicycles; in areas where conditions permit, covered walkways may directly connect the stop with surrounding buildings. Rail transit travel scenarios. At rail transit entrances and exits, priority should be given to traffic gathering and dispersal functions, while coordinating the needs of special groups, and providing plaza space for gathering and dispersal, a clear wayfinding signage system, small resting spaces, and a complete barrier-free facility system. Concentrated parking areas for non-motorized vehicles, public bicycles, and shared bicycles shall be set up, and emergency evacuation routes shall be clearly marked. In areas where conditions permit, corner plazas and pocket parks may be added; it is encouraged to integrate breakfast stalls, convenience stores, and other convenience service facilities with station entrances and exits, and to provide covered walkways between rail transit stations and surrounding public buildings. (5) Work scenarios. — 8 — Express delivery and meal delivery scenarios. Based on the needs of waiting and delivery services for express delivery and meal delivery, dedicated temporary parking spaces shall be delineated at the entrances and exits of large commercial facilities. Shopping malls and stores are encouraged to set up rest areas for couriers and meal delivery riders, as well as shared toilets, to create a harmonious street atmosphere. In areas where conditions permit, existing street facilities such as newsstands may be integrated to arrange service stations in a coordinated manner, providing one-stop solutions for various needs during work, such as water replenishment and charging, while also offering shelter from wind and rain.
